DHphsnW-nYo.html:
Growth adaptations

Essential knowledge

Organ is in homeostasis with stress placed on it

Increase, decrease, or change in stress on an organ can result in cellular adaptations

Cellular adaptations

Hypertrophy

Hyperplasia

Atrophy

Metaplasia

Cellular adaptations

Physiologic

Pathologic

Hypertrophy

Hypertrophy is increase in cell size

Caused by increase in stress

It can be physiologic or pathologic

Patrick J. Lynch, medical illustrator, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of hypertrophy

Cardiac hypertrophy: Occur due to stretch

Release of mediators that stimulate cell growth (growth factors and hormones) => turn on signal transduction => induce expression of genes => genes encode number of cellular proteins => one result is synthesis of myofilaments which increases force generated with each contraction => cell meets increased work demands

Other mechanism is maybe the switch of contractile proteins from adult to fetal or neonatal forms (e.g. switch of α myosin heavy chain to β myosin heavy chain) => this will produce slower and stronger contractions

Hypertrophy

Pathologic hypertrophy if not relieved can progress to cell injury and cell death

Hyperplasia

Hyperplasia is increase in the number of cells in an organ

It can be physiologic or pathologic

Pathologic hyperplasia vs cancer: responsive vs unresponsive to regulatory signals

Atrophy

Atrophy is reduced organ size caused by reduction in size and number of cells

Atrophy can be physiologic or pathologic

Mechanism of atrophy

Combination of decreased protein synthesis and increased protein degradation

Decrease protein synthesis is due to reduced metabolic activity

Protein degradation occur mainly by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway

Atrophy also accompanied by increased autophagy

Metaplasia

Metaplasia is a change in which one adult cell type is replaced by another adult cell type

Caused by change in stress

Mechanism of metaplasia

Reprogramming of stem cells

Examples of metaplasia

Respiratory epithelium metaplasia from ciliated columnar to stratified squamous epithelium due to prolonged cigarette smoking

Lower esophagus stratified squamous metaplasia to intestinal type columnar epithelium due to chronic gastric reflux

Examples of metaplasia

Keratomalacia: squamous epithelium of conjunctiva undergoes metaplasia to stratified keratinizing squamous epithelium

Myositis ossificans

Sara Bijan, Oliver R Filutowski, and Sara Safari, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Malignant transformation in metaplasia

If the causes that led to metaplasia are persistent then it may predispose to malignant transformation of the epithelium

kHhJRk4qxPQ.html:
Cell Injury

Cell injury

Cell injury occurs when stress exceeds cell’s ability to adapt

Likelihood of injury depends on

Type of stress

Severity of stress

Type of cell affected

Causes of cell injury

Hypoxia

Infection

Toxins

Immunologic reactions

Genetic mutations

Nutritional imbalances

Physical agents

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Hızır Erdem Uygun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Different injurious stimuli

Result in a similar sequence of alterations in most cell types

LiVolsi VA and Baloch ZW, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Hypoxia

Low oxygen delivery to tissues

Causes of hypoxia

Ischemia

Hypoxemia

Decreased O2 carrying capacity of the blood

Ischemia

Decreased blood flow through an organ

Hypoxemia

low partial pressure of O2 in blood (PaO2 < 60 mmHg , SaO2 < 90%)

Decrease O2 carrying capacity

Arises with Hb loss or dysfunction

Examples: Anemia and CO poisoning and Methemoglobinemia

Anemia

Decrease in RBC mass

PaO2 normal , SaO2 normal

CO poisoning

CO binds Hb Stronger than O2

PaO2 normal, SaO2 decreased

exposures include smoke from fires and exhaust from cars or gas heaters

Clinical features

Classic finding is cherry red appearance of skin

Early sign of exposure is headache

Significant exposure can lead to coma and death

Methemoglobinemia

Iron in heme is oxidized to Fe+3 , which cannot bind O2

PaO2 is normal , SaO2 is decreased

seen with oxidant stress (e.g. sulfa and nitrate drugs) or in newborns

Clinical Features and Treatment

Classic finding is cyanosis with chocolate colored blood

treatment is IV methylene blue which helps reduce Fe3+ back to Fe 2+ state

Hypoxia

Hypoxia impairs oxidative phosphorylation

Results in decreased ATP

Low ATP

Low ATP disrupts key cellular functions

Na+ - k+ pump

Ca2+ pump

Aerobic glycolysis

Initial phase of injury is reversible

Hallmark is cellular swelling

Leads to loss of

Microvilli

Membrane blebbing

Swelling of RER

LiVolsi VA and Baloch ZW, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Other features of reversible cell injury

Fatty changes

Mitochondrial changes include swelling , appearance of phospholipid rich amorphous densities

Nuclear alterations:

clumping of chromatin

Appearance of myelin figures

ROBBINS & KUMAR BASIC PATHOLOGY (11th edition, 2022)

Cell death

Persistent or excessive injury => irreversible injury (cell death)

Hallmark is membrane damage

ROBBINS & KUMAR BASIC PATHOLOGY (11th edition, 2022)

Cell death

I-_HV25j_9s.html:
Cell death

Stress on cell => growth adaptations

Severe stress on cell => cell injury => cell death

ROBBINS & KUMAR BASIC PATHOLOGY (11th edition, 2022)

Morphologic hallmark of cell death

Loss of nucleus via

Pyknosis

Karyorrhexis

Karyolysis

Mechanisms of cell death

Necrosis

Apoptosis

Necrosis

Death of a large group of cells followed by acute inflammation

Due to underlying pathologic process; never physiologic

It is the major pathway of cell death in many commonly encountered injuries

Necrosis

Divided into several types based on gross features

Coagulative necrosis

Liquefactive necrosis

Gangrenous necrosis

Fat necrosis

Fibrinoid necrosis

Coagulative necrosis

Cell shape and organ structure are preserved because the injury denatures structural proteins and enzymes limiting proteolysis of dead tissue for days to weeks after injury

Necrotic tissue that remains firm

Nucleus disappears

Coagulative necrosis

Dead tissue is digested by lysosomal enzymes of recruited leukocytes and cellular debris is removed by phagocytosis after several days to weeks

Characteristic of ischemic infarction of any organ except brain

Calicut Medical College, CC BY-SA 4.0. via Wikimedia Commons

Ed Uthman (Pathologist), CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Coagulative necrosis

Area of infarcted tissue is often wedge-shaped and pale

Dentl college survival kit, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Red infarction

It occurs if blood re enters a loosely organized tissue

Example: red infarction of the testicle

RWhitwam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Liquefactive necrosis

Necrotic tissue that becomes liquefied

Enzymatic digestion of cells and proteins results in liquefaction

ROBBINS & KUMAR BASIC PATHOLOGY (11th edition, 2022)

Occurs in

Brain infarction

Abscess

Pancreatitis

Gangrenous necrosis

A term that refers to coagulative necrosis of a limb (generally lower leg) and GI tract when blood supply has been lost

It is on two types: dry gangrene, but if superimposed infection occurs then liquefactive necrosis occurs (wet gangrene)

Narraburra, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Caseous necrosis

Necrotic tissue appears as friable yellow-white (cheese like)

Combination of coagulative and liquefactive necrosis

Occurs in granulomatous inflammation due to TB or fungal infection

Yale Rosen from USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Fat necrosis

Focal areas of necrotic adipose tissue

Appears as chalky white lesions due to released fatty acids combining with calcium

ROBBINS & KUMAR BASIC PATHOLOGY (11th edition, 2022)

Fat necrosis

Occur in

Trauma to fat (e.g. breast)

Pancreatic mediated damage of peripancreatic fat

Saponification

Fatty acids released by trauma or lipase join with calcium

Example of dystrophic calcification

Fibrinoid necrosis

Necrotic damage to blood vessel wall

Leaking of proteins into vessel wall results in bright pink staining

Characteristic of malignant hypertension or vasculitis

Angela Xue, Adele Bernard, Vanessa Moreno, Lindsey Phillips, Evan Raff, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Apoptosis

Energy-dependent, genetically programmed cell death

Involves single cells or small groups of cells

Apoptosis

Examples

Endometrial shedding during menstrual cycle

Removal of cells during embryogenesis

CD8+ T cell- mediated killing of virally infected cells

Slide 23

Apoptosis Morphology

Dying cell shrinks (becomes eosinophilic)

Nucleus condenses and fragments

Apoptotic bodies fall from cell and are removed by macrophages; not followed by inflammation

Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, eleventh edition

Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, eleventh edition

Apoptosis is mediated by caspases

Activate proteases (break down cytoskeleton)

Activate endonucleases (break down DNA)

Caspases are activated by multiple pathways

Intrinsic mitochondrial pathway

Extrinsic receptor-ligand pathway

Cytotoxic CD8+ T cell pathway

Intrinsic mitochondrial pathway

Cellular injury, DNA damage, or decreased hormonal stimulation inactivates Bcl2

Cytochrome c leaks from inner mitochondrial matrix into cytoplasm

Extrinsic receptor-ligand pathway

FAS ligand binds FAS death receptor (CD 95) on target cell

TNF binds TNF receptor on target cell

Cytotoxic CD8+ T cell pathway

Perforins create pores in membrane of target cell

Granzyme enters pores and activates caspases

Slide 31

Necrosis Apoptosis
Cell size Enlarged (swelling) Reduced (shrinkage)
Nucleus Pyknosis => karyorrhexis => karyolysis Fragmentation into nucleosome sized fragments
Plasma membrane Disrupted Intact; altered structure
cellular contents Enzymatic digestion Intact
Inflammation Yes No
Physiologic vs pathologic Always pathologic Often physiologic

Other mechanisms of cell death

Necroptosis

Pyroptosis

Ferroptosis

Autophagy

Lysosomal digestion of cell’s own components

It is a survival mechanism in times of nutrient deprivation that enables the cell to live by eating its own components

Involves the formation of autophagic vacuole

Robbins & Kumar Basic Pathology, eleventh edition

Mechanisms of cell injury

Mitochondrial dysfunction and damage

Oxidative stress

Amyloidosis

Thanks to our members

Oxidative stress

Cellular damage induced by accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), a form of free radical

Free radicals are Chemical species with unpaired electron in outer orbit

Physiologic generation

Oxidative phosphorylation

Cytochrome c oxidase transfers electrons to O2 during oxidative phosphorylation

Partial reduction yields O2-, H2O2 and OH radicals

Pathologic generation

Ionizing radiation

Inflammation

Metals (e.g., copper and iron)

Drugs and toxins (e.g., acetaminophen)

Free radical damage

Peroxidation of lipids

Crosslinking of proteins

Oxidation of DNA

Elimination of free radicals

Antioxidants

Metal carrier proteins

Enzymes

Enzymes

SOD

Catalase

Glutathione peroxidase

Examples of Free radical injury

CCl4

Reperfusion injury

Laboratory of Experimental Pathology, Division of Intramural Research, NIEHS (NIH), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Examples of Free radical injury

CCl4

Reperfusion injury

Slide 12

Free radical Mechanism of production Mechanisms of removal Pathologic effects
Superoxide (O2-) Incomplete reduction of O2 during oxidative phosphorylation; by phagocyte oxidase in leukocytes Conversion to H2O2 and O2 by superoxide dismutase Direct damaging effects on lipids (peroxidation), proteins, and DNA
Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) Mostly from superoxide by action of SOD Conversion to H2O and O2 by catalaseCan be converted to OH and CIO- , which destroy microbes and cells
Hydroxyl radical (OH) Produced from H2O, H2O2, and O2- by various chemical reactions Conversion to H2O by glutathione peroxidase Direct damaging effects on lipids, proteins, and DNA

I0ygFfqwhHw.html:
Slide 1

Amyloid

Misfolded protein that deposits in extracellular space

Damages tissues

Amyloidosis

Multiple proteins can deposit as amyloid

β- pleated sheet configuration

Congo red staining and apple-green birefringence under polarized light

Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Ed Uthman from Houston, TX, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Classification

Primary amyloidosis

Systemic deposition of AL amyloid, derived from Ig light chain

Associated with plasma cell proliferations

Organs affected include heart, GI tract, respiratory tract, peripheral nerves, skin and tongue

Tokenzero, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Reactive Systemic Amyloidosis (secondary)

Systemic deposition of AA amyloid derived from SAA

SAA is an acute phase reactant that is increased in chronic inflammatory states, malignancy

Organs affected include kidneys, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, adrenal glands and thyroid glands

Heredofamilial Amyloidosis

Variety of familial forms of amyloidosis are described but most are rare, the most common being familial Mediterranean fever (FMF)

FMF is autosomal recessive, autoinflammatory syndrome, characterized by excessive production of cytokine IL-1

Familial Mediterranean Fever

Presents with episodes of fever and acute serosal inflammation

High SAA during attacks deposits as AA amyloid

Organs affected include kidneys, blood vessels, spleen, respiratory tract, and (rarely) liver.

Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (Familial amyloid cardiomyopathy)

Mutated serum transthyretin deposits in heart

Leads to restrictive cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias

4% of African Americans carry mutated gene and penetrance differs substantially among individuals; some have severe disease while others have no disease at all

Senile systemic amyloidosis (Senile cardiac amyloidosis)

Non mutated serum transthyretin (TTR) deposits occur with aging

Usually asymptomatic but if symptomatic it present with restrictive cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias

Clinical findings

Renal involvement: most affected organ, proteinuria

Cardiac involvement: Restrictive cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia

GI involvement: Tongue enlargement, malabsorption, and hepatosplenomegaly

Vascular involvement: vessels fragility

Diagnosis

Dx is based on histopathology: H&E stain shows amyloid as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline extracellular substance, while it appears red in color under ordinary light using Congo red stain and apple green birefringence under polarized light using the same stain

Commonly biopsied sites include the kidneys, rectum, gingival tissue, abdominal fat pads

Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Diagnosis

Serum and urine protein electrophoresis

Bone marrow examination

Scintigraphy with radiolabeled SAP

Mass spectrometry

Damaged organs must be transplanted

Amyloid cannot be removed

Prognosis

Prognosis of generalized amyloidosis is poor

AL amyloidosis without MM median survival is 2 years after diagnosis while those with MM have worse prognosis

Reactive systemic amyloidosis has a better prognosis generally

Localized amyloidosis

Amyloid deposition usually localized to a single organ

Lung, larynx, skin, urinary bladder, tongue and region around the eye maybe affected

Frequently, infiltrates of lymphocytes and plasma cells a/w these amyloid masses

In some cases, the amyloid consist of AL amyloid, and therefore represent a localized form of plasma cell derived amyloid

Insulin Dependent Diabetes Mellitus

Amylin deposits in islets of pancreas

Derived from insulin

Medullary carcinoma of thyroid

Calcitonin deposits within tumor

Alzheimer disease

Aβ amyloid deposits in brain, forming amyloid plaques

Derived from β- amyloid precursor protein (on chromosome 21)

Dialysis-associated amyloidosis

β2- macroglobulin deposits in joints

outline.summary: Misfolded protein that deposits in extracellular space Damages tissues

outline.summary: Multiple proteins can deposit as amyloid β- pleated sheet configuration Congo red staining and apple-green birefringence under polarized light Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Primary amyloidosis
outline.summary: Systemic deposition of AL amyloid, derived from Ig light chain Associated with plasma cell proliferations Organs affected include heart, GI tract, respiratory tract, peripheral nerves, skin and tongue Tokenzero, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Reactive Systemic Amyloidosis (secondary)
outline.summary: Systemic deposition of AA amyloid derived from SAA SAA is an acute phase reactant that is increased in chronic inflammatory states, malignancy Organs affected include kidneys, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, adrenal glands and thyroid glands

outline.heading: Heredofamilial Amyloidosis
outline.summary: Variety of familial forms of amyloidosis are described but most are rare, the most common being familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) FMF is autosomal recessive, autoinflammatory syndrome, characterized by excessive production of cytokine IL-1

outline.heading: Familial Mediterranean Fever
outline.summary: Presents with episodes of fever and acute serosal inflammation High SAA during attacks deposits as AA amyloid Organs affected include kidneys, blood vessels, spleen, respiratory tract, and (rarely) liver.

outline.summary: Mutated serum transthyretin deposits in heart Leads to restrictive cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias 4% of African Americans carry mutated gene and penetrance differs substantially among individuals; some have severe disease while others have no disease at all

outline.summary: Non mutated serum transthyretin (TTR) deposits occur with aging Usually asymptomatic but if symptomatic it present with restrictive cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias

iFo2ROztdGs.html:
Thanks to our members

Mechanism of Intracellular Accumulations

Inadequate removal and degradation of an endogenous substance

Excessive production

Deposition of abnormal exogenous material

Fatty Change (Steatosis)

Abnormal accumulation of triglycerides within cells

Most often seen in the liver but also could occur in the heart, skeletal muscle, kidney and other organs

Mostly caused by alcohol abuse and diabetes

Calicut Medical College, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Cholesterol & Cholesteryl Esters

Cellular cholesterol metabolism is highly regulated

Phagocytic cells may become overloaded with lipids in pathologic conditions characterized by increased intake or decreased catabolism of lipids (e.g., atherosclerosis)

Calicut Medical College, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Proteins

Less common than lipid accumulations

In nephrotic syndrome, excessive amounts of resorbed albumin accumulate in vesicles in the tubular epithelial cells seen as pink, hyaline cytoplasmic droplets

Marked accumulation of immunoglobulins in the rough ER of some plasma cells forming rounded, eosinophilic Russell bodies

Mangla A, Agarwal N, Kim GJ, Catchatourian R, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Glycogen

Associated with abnormalities in the metabolism of either glucose or glycogen

Examples: Diabetes & Glycogen storage diseases

Jensflorian, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Pigments

Pigments are colored substances that could be endogenous or exogenous

Carbon

Lipofuscin

Melanin

Hemosiderin

Carbon

Most common accumulated exogenous pigment (air pollutant)

When inhaled, it is phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages and transported to lymphatic channels to the regional lymph nodes

Calicut Medical College, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Lipofuscin

Insoluble brownish- yellow granular intracellular pigment

Accumulates in heart, liver, and brain

Occur with aging (wear and tear pigment)

Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Melanin

Brown-black pigment that is synthesized by melanocytes

Acts as a screen against harmful ultraviolet radiation

Calicut Medical College, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Hemosiderin

Yellow to brown granular pigment derived from hemoglobin

Accumulates in tissues where there is a local or systemic excess of iron

Hemosiderin accumulations are usually pathologic except small amounts in bone marrow, spleen and liver phagocytes

Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Slide 1

Slide 2

Slide 3

A 60 years old female presented with severe chest pain for the past 3 hours. On physical examination she is afebrile but has tachycardia. Labs show elevated serum troponin. A coronary angiogram is performed, and it reveals > 95 % occlusion of the left anterior descending artery.

In this setting, an irreversible injury to myocardial fibers will have occurred when which of the following cellular changes happen:

Glycogen stores are depleted

Cytoplasmic sodium increases

Nuclei undergo karyorrhexis

Intracellular pH decreases

Blebs form on cell membranes

Slide 4

A 68-year-old man with a history of CAD suffers and acute MI. Thrombolytic therapy with tPA is administered to restore coronary blood flow. Despite this treatment, the degree of myocardial fiber injury may increase because of which of the following:

Cytoskeletal intermediate filament loss

Decreased intracellular pH from anaerobic glycolysis

Increased free radical formation

Mitochondrial swelling

Nuclear chromatin clumping

Slide 5

A 50-year-old male patient presented with black appearance to his first, second and third toes of his left foot. On physical examination, the toes are cold and have no sensation to touch. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are not palpable on the left foot. Amputation is performed.

In which condition these findings are most typical of:

Diabetes mellitus

Gout

Blunt force trauma

AIDS

Rheumatoid arthritis

Slide 6

At the end of a menstrual cycle, the endometrium sloughs. Examination of the endometrium microscopically shows cellular fragmentation. What is the most likely trigger of apoptosis in these endometrial cells:

Acute inflammation

Hypoxia

P53 protein accumulation

Decreased estrogen

Anaerobic glycolysis

A 60-year-old male patient who smoked 2 packs of cigarettes per day for the past 30 years. He has had chronic cough for the past 10 years.

Recently he noted increased sputum production, on examination he has few crackles heard over lung bases. Bronchoscopy with biopsy reveals bronchial epithelium with squamous metaplasia. What statement best describe these findings:

Physiologic process of aging

Irreversible process, even after smoking cessation

Metastasis to the lung

Infection

Thromboembolism with infarction

Slide 8

In an experiment, a tissue preparation is subjected to oxidant stress. There are increased numbers of free radicals generated within the cells. Generation of which of the following enzymes within these cells is the most likely protective mechanism to reduce the number of free radicals:

Glutathione peroxidase

Hydrogen peroxide

NADPH oxidase

Myeloperoxidase

Slide 9

A 60-year-old male patient diagnosed with Hodgkin’s lymphoma involving the lymph nodes in para-aortic region. He is treated with chemotherapeutic medication which result in shrinking of the lymph nodes size as documented on abdominal CT scans. By which of the following mechanisms the neoplasm decreased in size:

Coagulative necrosis

Mitochondrial poisoning

Phagocytosis

Acute inflammation

Apoptosis

Slide 10

A 40-year-old female patient presented with burning substernal pain following meals for the past 4 years. Upper GI endoscopy is performed, and biopsies are taken showing the presence of columnar epithelium with goblet cells on the lower part of esophagus above the esophagogastric junction, there is no mass lesion, no ulceration or hemorrhage noted. Which of the following is the most likely mucosal alteration occurred:

Dysplasia

Hyperplasia

Carcinoma

Ischemia

Metaplasia

Slide 11

A 71-year-old female patient presented with weakness on her right arm and right leg. Cerebral angiogram shows occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery, and an echocardiogram reveals a thrombus within the left atrium. Which of the following most likely pathologic alterations occurred in her brain:

Liquefactive necrosis

Coagulative necrosis

Loss of glial cells

Wet gangrene with secondary bacterial infection

Fat necrosis

A 30-year-old male patient presented with a 5 * 5 cm purple in color skin lesion on the thigh, after getting struck with falling tennis rack 2 days ago.

Which of the following substances has most likely accumulated in the site of injury to produce a yellow-brown color at that site 16 days later:

Lipofuscin

Bilirubin

Melanin

Hemosiderin

Glycogen

Slide 1

Slide 2

Slide 3

A 61-year-old female patient develops diarrhea and abdominal pain, 3 weeks after starting radiation therapy for Pancreatic Cancer. Physical examination shows abdominal tenderness & sigmoidoscopy reveals hyperemia, edema, and ulceration of the intestinal mucosa. Radiation enteritis is suspected. Which of the following is the most likely primary mechanism responsible for intestinal changes in this patient:

Generation of reactive oxygen species

Increased activity of ubiquitin-proteosome system

Inhibition of DNA polymerase

Inhibition of thymidylate synthesis

Prevention of microtubule assembly

Slide 4

Slide 5

A 58-year-old man presented with worsening cough, SOB, and episodic hemoptysis during the past 8 months. The patient lost 30 pounds over the same period without any change in his diet or activity level. He has a 60-pack-year smoking history. The patient look cachectic with temporal wasting and generalized loss of muscle mass. CXR reveals large mediastinal mass, which of the following cellular processes is most likely responsible for his muscle loss:

Covalent attachment of ubiquitin to muscle proteins

Plasma membrane rupture with leakage of cellular contents

Plasma membrane instability due to defective dystrophin

Progressive shortening of chromosomal telomeres

Reprogramming of undifferentiated mesenchymal cells

Slide 6

Slide 7

A 73-year-old male patient with a history of atrial fibrillation admitted to ER due to left leg pain and numbness, doppler US shows occluding thrombus and embolectomy is performed. Post procedure dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses become palpable (they were absent before), several hours later, patient begin experiencing severe left calf pain, O/E the left calf is swollen, tense and tender and the pain worsen with dorsiflexion of the left foot. Injury of the re perfused muscle is suspected due to overproduction of ROS. Which of the following enzyme help neutralize these toxic molecules:

Cytochrome oxidase

Cytochrome P450

Myeloperoxidase

NADPH oxidase

Superoxide dismutase

Slide 8

Slide 9

A 65-year-old male patient presented to ER with acute severe right flank pain with nausea and vomiting for the past hour. His PMH include prostate cancer and membranous nephropathy. On physical examination, there is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows hematuria. Contrast enhanced CT reveals a wedge-shaped perfusion defect in the right kidney. The affected tissue developed which type of histologic change over the next several days:

Caseous necrosis

Coagulative necrosis

Fat necrosis

Fibrinoid necrosis

Liquefactive necrosis

Slide 10

Slide 11

Slide 12

Slide 13

A 67-year-old male patient presented to ER with right sided weakness and difficulty speaking. He has a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and not adherent to medical therapy. Physical examination shows right sided hemiplegia, hemisensory loss and aphasia. Despite treatment, the patient didn’t improve. Over the next week, which of the following processes is most likely to occur in the affected brain region:

Accumulation of fibrin-like material in vessel walls

Formation of a necrotic focus surrounded by epithelioid macrophages

Deposition of fatty acid and calcium complexes

Hydrolytic enzyme induced tissue digestion

Tissue necrosis with preservation of cellular architecture

Slide 14

Slide 15

Slide 16

Slide 17

Slide 18

Slide 19

An experiment is conducted to determine if lipid peroxidation is lessened by the effects of vitamin E ingestion. Which of the following is primarily involved in generation of lipid peroxides, the formation of which is inhibited by the vitamin E:

Glutathione

Ionized calcium

Lactate

Ferric iron

Lipase

Slide 20

Slide 21

A 25-year-old female had chronic renal failure due to Goodpasture syndrome. Her blood pressure is 170/110 mmHg. Labs show her BUN is over 100 mg/dL and she is on hemodialysis. A chest radiograph show an enlarged heart. The size of her heart is most likely to be the result of which of the following processes involving myocardial fibers:

Hypertrophy

Fatty infiltration

Hyperplasia

Fatty degeneration

Edema

Slide 22

Slide 23

A 10-year-old boy has had multiple episodes of ear pain accompanied by fever. On examination his right tympanic membrane is bulging with yellow exudate. A year later he developed conductive hearing loss on the same ear, and head CT scan shows a mass in the right middle ear.

Which of the following materials is most likely to be seen in the tissue curetted from his middle ear:

Lipofuscin pigment

Russel bodies

Neutrophil granules

Cholesterol crystals

Anthracotic pigment

Slide 24

Slide 25

A 50-year-old male patient with chronic cough has squamous cell carcinoma diagnosed in his left lung. While performing a pneumonectomy, the thoracic surgeon notes that hilar lymph nodes are small and look black in color.

Which of the following is the most likely cause for the black appearance of his hilar lymph nodes:

Anthracotic pigment

Lipochrome deposits

Melanin accumulation

Hemosiderosis

Metastatic carcinoma

Slide 26

Slide 27

A 45-year-old female patient has sudden onset severe abdominal pain. On physical examination she has diffuse tenderness in all abdomen, guarding and rigidity. Her labs show elevated lipase and LDH with normal ALT and AST. An abdominal CT scan reveals peritoneal fluid collections and enlargement with decreased attenuation of the pancreas.

Which of the following cellular changes is most likely to accompany these findings:

Coagulative necrosis

Dry gangrene

Fat necrosis

Apoptosis

Liquefactive necrosis
